name: Sadyojyoti
summary: The earliest Siddhānta author whose works survive: philosophical treatises proving the soul and the Lord against Buddhists and others, and defining liberation as the soul's equality with Śiva; commentaries on the Svāyambhuva and (reportedly) the Raurava.
notes: Names his teacher as Ugrajyoti (moderate confidence). A commentary on the Raurava(sūtrasaṅgraha) is reported but not treated here (gap).

name: Ugrajyoti
summary: Named by Sadyojyoti as his teacher; no work of his survives.

name: Bṛhaspati (Saiddhāntika)
summary: An early Siddhānta authority cited by later exegetes (Rāmakaṇṭha, Abhinavagupta) as pre-dating or contemporary with Sadyojyoti; his work is lost except in citations (a title Śivatanu(śāstra) is associated with him — low confidence).
notes: Distinct from the Vedic Bṛhaspati and from the Lokāyata founder of the same name.

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika, author of the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, which explains the Āgama's doctrine of Lord, souls and bonds and defends the Siddhānta's realism; father of Rāmakaṇṭha II.

name: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (Rāmakaṇṭha II)
summary: The foremost Kashmirian exegete of the Siddhānta: commentaries on the Mataṅgapārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Sārdhatriśatikālottara, and Sadyojyoti's Nareśvaraparīkṣā, Mokṣakārikā and Paramokṣanirāsakārikā. He argued that mala is a substance removable only by Śiva's power in initiation, that the liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva, and answered the non-dualist Śaivas.
notes: Correction to the unit brief: 'Rāmakaṇṭha II' and 'Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha' are the same person (the Saiddhāntika son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha). He is distinct from Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha, author of the Spandakārikāvivṛti and a Gītā commentary (non-dualist milieu). Some scholars suggest the Śrīkaṇṭha of the Ratnatraya was his teacher (low confidence).

name: Śrīkaṇṭha (author of the Ratnatraya)
summary: Saiddhāntika author of the Ratnatraya on Śiva, Śakti and bindu, commented on by Aghoraśiva.
notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya, Śivādvaita). Possibly the Śrīkaṇṭha named as a teacher of Rāmakaṇṭha (low confidence).

name: Bhoja (Paramāra king of Dhārā)
summary: Scholar-king of Mālava, author of the Siddhānta manual Tattvaprakāśa and (attributed) the ritual Siddhāntasārapaddhati, as well as the Yoga commentary Rājamārtaṇḍa.

name: Śrīkumāra
summary: Commentator (Tātparyadīpikā) on Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa.

name: Somaśambhu
summary: Abbot of a Śaiva monastery in central India (the Golagī maṭha tradition is usually named — moderate confidence), author of the most influential Siddhānta ritual manual, the Somaśambhupaddhati (Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī), completed 1095/96.

name: Aghoraśiva
summary: Twelfth-century Śaiva ācārya of Chidambaram (Āmardaka lineage — moderate confidence) whose ritual manual Kriyākramadyotikā (1157/58) and commentaries (on the Mṛgendravṛtti and six of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa treatises) fixed the dualist reading of the Siddhānta followed by South Indian temple priests.
notes: Corrected: his Aṣṭaprakaraṇa commentaries cover six treatises (not the Mokṣakārikā or Paramokṣanirāsakārikā).

name: Trilocanaśiva
summary: Twelfth-century South Indian Saiddhāntika, author of the Siddhāntasārāvalī and the Prāyaścittasamuccaya (and reportedly a commentary on the Somaśambhupaddhati — low confidence).

name: Śivāgrayogin
summary: Sixteenth-century bilingual Siddhānta scholar of the Tamil country who wrote in Sanskrit (the Śaivaparibhāṣā; a commentary on the Sanskrit Śivajñānabodha) and in Tamil (a commentary on the Civañāṉa Cittiyār).

name: Tirumūlar
summary: Author of the Tirumantiram, one of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars.
alt_names: Cuntaraṉātar (his name before entering Mūlaṉ's body, per the Periya Purāṇam)

realization_account.text: A yogī-disciple of Nandi from Kailāsa, travelling south to meet Agastya, found the herdsman Mūlaṉ dead at Cāttaṉūr with his cows grieving; he entered Mūlaṉ's body by yogic power to console them, later found his own body gone by Śiva's will, and sat in yoga under a pipal tree at Tiruvāvaṭuturai, singing one verse a year for three thousand years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
summary: One of the three Tēvāram poets (Tirumuṟai 4–6), a former Jain monk (Tarumacēṉar) who returned to Śaivism; exemplar of the servant's path (dāsa-mārga, caryā); famed for temple service (clearing the temple grounds) and hymns of defiance and surrender.

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of the Pallava Mahendravarman I (r. c. 600–630)

realization_account.text: Raised a Śaiva and cared for by his sister Tilakavati, he became a Jain monk; struck by an incurable colic he returned to Tilakavati at Tiruvatikai, received the sacred ash, and sang his first hymn, and the pain left him. The Jain-influenced Pallava king had him shut in a lime-kiln, fed poison, trampled by an elephant and thrown into the sea tied to a stone; he survived each by singing Śiva's names, floated ashore, and the king turned Śaiva. He died at Tiruppukalūr merging with Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tiruñāṉacampantar
summary: Child-saint and the most prolific Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 1–3); exemplar of the son's path (satputra-mārga, kriyā); champion of Śaivism against the Jains at Madurai.

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of Appar, the Pāṇṭiya Neṭumāṟaṉ and Ciṟuttoṇṭar (Vātāpi, 642)

places: Nallūr Perumaṇam (union with Śiva at his wedding)

realization_account.text: At three, left on the tank's edge at Cīkāḻi, he cried and Umā fed him the milk of divine knowledge in a golden cup; asked who had fed him, he sang his first hymn pointing to Śiva and Umā. He went on pilgrimage with the bard Tirunīlakaṇṭa Yāḻppāṇar, was invited to Madurai by the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār and the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, cured the king's fever with sacred ash, and won the fire and water ordeals against the Jains. At sixteen, at his wedding at Nallūr Perumaṇam, he entered a divine light with his bride and all the guests.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cuntaramūrtti (Cuntarar)
summary: Third Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 7); exemplar of the friend's path (sakhā-mārga, yoga); author of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai, the list of devotees on which the cult of the sixty-three rests.

realization_account.text: An Ādiśaiva boy of Tirunāvalūr adopted by the chieftain Naracinka Muṉaiyaraiyar; on his wedding day an old brahmin produced a deed showing Cuntarar's grandfather had pledged his line as the brahmin's slaves; followed to Tiruveṇṇeynallūr, the old man vanished into the temple — Śiva himself — and Cuntarar sang 'Pittā' ('Madman!'). Śiva later acted as his messenger to his wife Paravai. With Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ he rode to Kailāsa on a white elephant sent by Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumuṟai 8); the fourth samayācārya, exemplar of the true path (san-mārga, jñāna). Not among the sixty-three.

tradition.text: placed before the Tēvāram poets by much of the tradition

realization_account.text: Chief minister of the Pāṇṭiya king (named Arimarttaṉa in later accounts), sent with treasure to buy horses, he met Śiva as a guru under a kuruntha tree at Tirupperunturai, received initiation and spent the treasure on a temple. Imprisoned, he was saved when Śiva turned foxes into horses (which became foxes again), and when Śiva, hired as a labourer by the old woman Vanti to repair the Vaikai embankment, received the king's blow that struck every creature. At Chidambaram he defeated Buddhists from Laṅkā in debate; Śiva, as a brahmin, wrote down the Tiruvācakam and signed it; asked its meaning, he pointed to Naṭarāja and merged in him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: His absence from Cuntarar's list is used by scholars to date him after Cuntarar.

name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Minister of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (Anapāyaṉ), author of the Periya Purāṇam, the twelfth Tirumuṟai.

realization_account.text: Seeing the king delight in the Jain epic Cīvakacintāmaṇi, he turned him to the lives of Śiva's devotees; at Chidambaram Śiva gave him the first word 'ulakelām' and he completed the work in a year.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Priest of Tirunāraiyūr who, by the tradition's account, recovered the Tēvāram at Chidambaram and arranged the first eleven Tirumuṟai; author of ten works in the eleventh, including the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti.

realization_account.text: As a boy he fed the Gaṇeśa (Poḷḷāppiḷḷaiyār) of Tirunāraiyūr, who ate and taught him; guided by that Gaṇeśa he found the hymns in a sealed chamber at Chidambaram, half eaten by termites — what remained was what the Lord wished preserved.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Founder of the Tamil Siddhānta school; author of the Civañāṉa Pōtam; head of the lineage of 'outer' teachers (puṟaccantāṉam).

realization_account.text: Born to a childless Vēḷāḷa couple after they bathed at Tiruveṇkāṭu as Campantar's hymn instructed, and named after its Lord; as a child he was taught by the sage Parañcōti from Kailāsa, who named him Meykaṇṭār, 'he who saw the truth'. He gathered 49 disciples; the learned family priest Aruṇanti, who came to test the child, became his foremost disciple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (guru of Meykaṇṭār)
summary: The sage from Kailāsa who, in the tradition's account, taught the child Meykaṇṭār; last of the 'inner' lineage (akaccantāṉam) of Nandi, Sanatkumāra and Satyajñānadarśin.
notes: Distinct from Parañcōti Muṉivar, author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam (tch:parancoti-tiruvilaiyatal).

name: Satyajñānadarśin
summary: Third teacher of the inner lineage of Tamil Siddhānta (after Nandi and Sanatkumāra), teacher of Parañcōti.

name: Nandi (Nandikeśvara)
summary: Śiva's chief attendant and doorkeeper at Kailāsa; in Tamil Siddhānta the first human-facing teacher of the inner lineage, and the guru of Tirumūlar.

name: Aruṇanti Civācāriyār
summary: Author of the Civañāṉa Cittiyār and Irupā Irupatu; a learned brahmin, family preceptor of Meykaṇṭār's father, who became Meykaṇṭār's chief disciple.

name: Maṉavācakaṅkaṭantār
summary: Disciple of Meykaṇṭār from Tiruvatikai, author of the Uṇmai Viḷakkam.

name: Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar
summary: Disciple of Aruṇanti and guru of Umāpati Civācāriyār; third of the four teachers of the outer lineage. No Meykaṇṭa treatise is his.

realization_account.text: Seeing the Chidambaram priest Umāpati carried in a palanquin with a torch in daylight, he called out 'a day-blind man riding a dead log'; stung, Umāpati followed him and became his disciple, eating food from his hand, for which the Tillai priests excluded him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Details of his caste and the palanquin story are given at low confidence (they come from later hagiography).

name: Umāpati Civācāriyār
summary: Chidambaram priest (Tillai dīkṣitar) turned disciple of Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar; author of eight of the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras (Civappirakācam, Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ, Viṉāveṇpā, Poṟṟippahṟoṭai, Koṭikkavi, Neñcuviṭu Tūtu, Uṇmai Neṟi Viḷakkam [disputed], Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam), of the Sanskrit Pauṣkarabhāṣya and Śataratnasaṅgraha, and of Tamil purāṇas of Chidambaram and the saints.

realization_account.text: Excluded by the Tillai priests, he lived at Koṟṟavaṉkuṭi; when the festival flag would not rise he sang the Koṭikkavi and it rose. Naṭarāja is said to have sent him a verse-letter ordering liberation for the outcaste Peṟṟāṉ Cāmpāṉ, and he granted release even to a thorn bush.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tiruviyalūr
summary: Author of the Tiruvuntiyār (c. 1147), earliest of the Meykaṇṭa Śāstras.

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tirukkaṭavūr
summary: Author of the Tirukkaḷiṟṟuppaṭiyār (c. 1177), a commentary in verse on the Tiruvuntiyār; in the teaching line of the Tiruviyalūr author (through Āḷuṭaiya Tēvanāyaṉār — low confidence).

name: Civañāṉa Muṉivar
summary: Monk of the Tiruvāvaṭuturai ātīṉam, the classical scholastic of Tamil Siddhānta: the Civañāṉa Māpāṭiyam and Ciṟṟurai on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, a commentary on the Cittiyār, the first part of the Kāñci Purāṇam, grammatical works and a Tamil rendering of the Tarkasaṅgraha.

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam)
summary: Author of the Tamil Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam on Śiva's sixty-four sports at Madurai.

name: Nakkīrar
summary: Poet of the Madurai academy in tradition; author of the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (Tirumuṟai 11). The Tiruviḷaiyāṭal story tells of his dispute with Śiva over a poem.

name: Tirumāḷikaittēvar
summary: First of the nine poets of the Tiruvicaippā (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Cēntaṉār
summary: Poet of the Tiruvicaippā and of the benedictory Tiruppallāṇṭu (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Karuvūrār (Karuvūrttēvar)
summary: Poet of Tiruvicaippā hymns (Tirumuṟai 9), including one on the Rājarājeśvaram at Tañcāvūr; identified by tradition with the Siddhar Karuvūrār.

name: Kaṇṭarātittar
summary: Cōḻa king (Gaṇḍarāditya, r. c. 950–957) and poet of a Tiruvicaippā hymn to Naṭarāja at Chidambaram.

name: Tiruvaḷḷuvar
summary: Author of the Tirukkuṟaḷ. His affiliation is contested (Jain, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, non-sectarian); the Jain tradition identifies him with Elācārya/Kundakunda; Tamil Śaivas honour him as Tiruvaḷḷuva Nāyaṉār.

tradition.text: Sangam age; Tamil Nadu's Tiruvaḷḷuvar era begins 31 BCE

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. CE (range proposed: 300 BCE–6th c. CE)

realization_account.text: Later legends make him a weaver of Mayilāppūr with a devoted wife Vācuki, and a son of the brahmin Pakavaṉ and the Pulaiya woman Āti (from the late Kapilar Akaval — low confidence); his Kuṟaḷ was the only work the academy's plank would bear.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: lineages records the traditions that have claimed him, not an established affiliation.

name: Parimēlaḻakar
summary: Author of the most celebrated commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ (and on the Paripāṭal); a Vaiṣṇava brahmin of Kāñcīpuram by tradition.
notes: Vaiṣṇava affiliation is traditional; the lineage ids are approximate.

name: Maṇakkuṭavar
summary: Author of the oldest surviving Kuṟaḷ commentary; his own affiliation (some say Jain) is uncertain.

name: Ārumuka Nāvalar
summary: Jaffna Śaiva reformer and scholar: prose catechisms of Śaiva Siddhānta, printed editions of Tamil Śaiva texts, schools, and polemic against Christian missionaries.

name: Maṟaimalai Aṭikaḷ
summary: Tamil scholar and Śaiva Siddhānta advocate, leader of the 'pure Tamil' movement; argued for an early date of Māṇikkavācakar and led the 1921 fixing of the Tiruvaḷḷuvar era.

name: Tirunīlakaṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A potter of Tillai who, reproached by his wife for his infidelity, vowed 'by Tirunīlakaṇṭam' never to touch her and kept the vow into old age; when Śiva as a yogī's begging bowl left in his keeping vanished, the couple had to bathe holding hands to prove their word — they held a stick between them, the vow was revealed, and they rose from the water young again.

name: Iyaṟpakai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who never refused a devotee; when Śiva came as a brahmin and asked for his wife, he gave her, fought off his kinsmen who tried to stop them, and escorted the pair out of town — whereupon Śiva revealed himself.

name: Iḷaiyāṉkuṭi Māṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A farmer who fed devotees until he was destitute; on a night of heavy rain he gathered the newly sown paddy from his field and pulled up his roof-beams for firewood to feed a guest, who was Śiva.

realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Meypporuḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.

realization_account.text: A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Viṟaṉmiṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A devotee who declared Cuntarar and even the Lord 'outside' the fold when Cuntarar passed the assembled devotees at Tiruvārūr without honouring them; this led Śiva to give Cuntarar the first line of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai.

realization_account.text: A devotee who declared Cuntarar and even the Lord 'outside' the fold when Cuntarar passed the assembled devotees at Tiruvārūr without honouring them; this led Śiva to give Cuntarar the first line of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Amarnīti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.

realization_account.text: A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Eṟipatta Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut down the royal elephant that had scattered the flowers gathered for Śiva by the devotee Civakāmi Āṇṭār, and its keepers; the king Pukaḻccōḻar offered his own life in atonement and Eṟipattar tried to take his own, until Śiva intervened and restored all.

realization_account.text: He cut down the royal elephant that had scattered the flowers gathered for Śiva by the devotee Civakāmi Āṇṭār, and its keepers; the king Pukaḻccōḻar offered his own life in atonement and Eṟipattar tried to take his own, until Śiva intervened and restored all.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ēṉātinātar Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A master of swordsmanship whose defeated rival Atisūraṉ smeared sacred ash on his forehead before their duel; seeing the ash, Ēṉātinātar lowered his guard and let himself be killed rather than strike a wearer of Śiva's sign.

name: Kaṇṇappa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A hunter who worshipped the liṅga of Kāḷahasti with meat he had tasted, water carried in his mouth and flowers from his hair, to the dismay of the temple priest Civakōcariyār; when blood flowed from the liṅga's eye he plucked out his own eye and set it there; when the other eye bled he placed his foot on it to mark the spot and began to cut out his second eye — Śiva stopped his hand crying 'Stay, Kaṇṇappa!' and took him to his side.

name: Kuṅkiliyakkalaya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He burned kuṅkiliyam incense before Śiva, sold all he had for it, and spent even his wife's marriage badge on incense; at Tiruppaṉantāḷ he straightened the leaning liṅga by pulling with a rope tied to his own neck.

realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Māṉakkañcāṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.

realization_account.text: A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Arivāṭṭāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He offered red rice, greens and tender mango daily; impoverished and faint, he stumbled and the offering fell into a crack in the earth, and he began to cut his throat with a sickle (arivāḷ) — Śiva's hand rose from the crack to stop him.

realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Āṉāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.

realization_account.text: A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mūrtti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who supplied sandal paste to the Madurai temple; when a Jain-favouring usurper stopped the supply he ground his own elbow on the stone; made king by Śiva's will, he ruled with the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa and matted hair as his crown and insignia.

name: Muruka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who wove flower garlands for Śiva; friend of Campantar, he attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who stood in a tank day and night reciting the Śrī Rudram until Śiva granted him release.

name: Nantaṉār (Tirunāḷaippōvār)
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pulaiya (outcaste) labourer who supplied leather and strings for temple drums; at Tiruppuṅkūr Śiva moved the bull Nandi aside so he could see; long saying 'I will go to Tillai tomorrow', he at last reached Chidambaram where, at Śiva's command conveyed to the priests, he passed through fire, rose as a brahmin sage and entered the sanctum, never to be seen again.

name: Tirukkuṟipputtoṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A washerman who washed devotees' clothes; Śiva as a poor ascetic left a garment that had to be dry by evening, rain fell, and he began to dash his head against the washing stone — Śiva's hand stopped him.

name: Caṇṭēcura Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin boy who, tending the village cows, made a sand liṅga and bathed it with their milk; when his father kicked over the milk pots he struck at his father's legs with the staff, which became an axe; Śiva made him Caṇṭēcuran, chief of his attendants, heir to his leftover garlands and offerings.

name: Kulacciṟai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Minister of the Pāṇṭiya king Neṭumāṟaṉ who, with the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār, invited Campantar to Madurai and served devotees of every birth.

name: Perumiḻalaikkuṟumpa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain devoted to Cuntarar; knowing by yoga that Cuntarar would leave for Kailāsa, he left his body through the crown of the head a day before, to reach Kailāsa first.

name: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant's wife who gave one of two mangoes to a hungry devotee; when her husband asked for the second, she prayed and a mango appeared; frightened, he left her and remarried. She asked Śiva to take her beauty and give her the form of a ghoul (pēy), climbed Kailāsa on her hands, and was greeted by Śiva as 'Mother' (Ammai); she asked for no rebirth — or, if born again, never to forget him — and to sing at his feet as he dances, which she does at Tiruvālaṅkāṭu.

name: Appūti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, without having met Appar, named his sons, water-sheds and alms-houses after him; when Appar visited, a son died of snakebite and the parents hid it to feed their guest; Appar sang and the boy revived.

name: Tirunīlanakka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin priest whose wife blew away a spider that fell on the liṅga; he rebuked her for defiling it, and Śiva showed him blisters everywhere on his body except where she had blown. He attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

name: Naminanti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, refused oil by Jains for the temple lamps at Tiruvārūr, lit them with water at Śiva's word, and they burned.

summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Angered that Cuntarar made the Lord his messenger to Paravai, he was struck by colic that only Cuntarar could cure; rather than be cured by him he tore out his own bowels; Cuntarar, arriving, was about to die with him, when Śiva revived Kalikkāmar and the two became friends.

name: Taṇṭiyaṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Born blind, he dug out the silted temple tank at Tiruvārūr guided by ropes and stakes, mocked by Jains; Śiva gave him sight and the Jains lost theirs (the account adds that they left the town).

summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs.
